title: How to Win the Largest Market in AI | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z argues AI inference has grown into a workload large and stable enough to justify custom, full-stack hardware rather than general-purpose GPUs, and frames its investment in chip startup Etched as a bet that production-at-scale, not chip design alone, is the moat in this market.

themes.theme: The specialization turn in computing history

insights.claim: Historically, when a computing workload becomes large enough and its shape stable enough, it migrates from general-purpose processors into custom hardware built specifically for it, as happened when graphics moved from CPUs to GPUs and networking packet-switching moved from CPUs to custom switch chips made by companies like Broadcom.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: This pattern is the analytical lens the authors use to justify betting on inference-specific chips now that inference has reached scale — investors should look for the next workload crossing this threshold.
insights.quote: the more important a workload, and the more stable its shape, the more sense it makes to build hardware in the image of the workload
insights.locator: In short: the more important a workload

insights.claim: The authors believe AI inference is now the most consequential computing workload of this era and is undergoing the same specialization shift that previously happened to graphics and networking.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Frames AI inference hardware as a large, durable investment category rather than a niche or transient trend.
insights.locator: We are witnessing this now for perhaps the most consequential workload

themes.theme: Inference demand and cost are going vertical

insights.claim: In May 2026, Google announced it was processing 3.2 quadrillion tokens per month across its products, roughly 300 times the volume it was processing two years earlier.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: A ~300x token-volume increase in two years quantifies how fast inference compute demand — and the associated capex/opex needs — is scaling for hyperscalers.
insights.quote: processing 3.2 quadrillion tokens per month across its products, roughly 300 times what it had been processing two years earlier
insights.locator: In May 2026, Google announced

insights.claim: OpenAI now has roughly a billion monthly active users and a rapidly growing coding agent platform in Codex, both driving heavy inference demand.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: User-scale growth at OpenAI is a direct proxy for inference compute and power demand that custom inference chips are meant to serve.
insights.locator: We see the same story with OpenAI

insights.claim: Anthropic has seen enormous growth in inference demand from its Claude Code product, adding to the broader surge in token consumption across AI platforms.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Coding-agent products are called out specifically as a fast-growing, latency-sensitive inference workload class worth tracking for compute demand signals.
insights.locator: We see the same story with OpenAI

insights.claim: Unlike training, which is a one-time, amortizable capital cost per model, inference is an ongoing operating cost that scales directly with usage — every ChatGPT question, API call, or agent action incurs a real-time compute cost, making inference effectively 'the COGS of intelligence.'
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Investors should model AI companies' inference costs as a recurring COGS line that scales with user growth, not a sunk capex item — margin structure depends heavily on inference efficiency.
insights.quote: Inference is the COGS of intelligence.
insights.locator: Inference, by contrast, is opex

insights.claim: Because AI data centers are now constrained by available power (watts) rather than by capital (dollars), any energy a general-purpose chip spends on flexibility the inference workload doesn't need is wasted, making tokens-per-watt the key efficiency metric for inference economics.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Tokens-per-watt is presented as the metric investors should use to evaluate competing inference hardware and site economics, given power is now the binding constraint.
insights.quote: Tokens per watt is the real currency of inference.
insights.locator: Data centers are now gated by watts

themes.theme: Why GPUs are structurally mismatched to inference

insights.claim: Generating each token requires streaming a model's entire weights (hundreds of gigabytes of parameters) plus a growing context-window cache out of memory while performing only a couple of simple operations per byte, meaning token generation is fundamentally memory-bound rather than compute-bound.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Explains mechanistically why memory bandwidth and interconnect design, not raw FLOPs, are the real bottleneck inference-specific chips need to solve.
insights.locator: Generating a token is less about arithmetic

insights.claim: Batching — serving many users' requests together to amortize the cost of reading model weights from memory — improves throughput but sells latency in exchange, a trade that fast-growing, latency-sensitive workloads like coding agents in tight loops and long-context reasoning cannot afford.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Signals that latency-sensitive agentic workloads are the segment most likely to abandon GPU-based batching in favor of purpose-built inference hardware first.
insights.quote: It buys throughput, but it does so by selling latency and making every inference workload slower.
insights.locator: The standard patch for this is what's called "batching"

themes.theme: Hyperscaler precedent and the gap it leaves open

insights.claim: Google began building custom AI silicon in the early 2010s with the TPU, and Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have since followed with their own custom inference chips; frontier labs like OpenAI are now following the same path.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Establishes custom silicon as an already-proven strategy among the largest AI players, reducing the risk that Etched's approach is unproven.
insights.locator: For neural networks, this transformation started

insights.claim: Hyperscaler custom silicon like Google's TPU is only accessible by renting, not by purchasing or racking in one's own data center, leaving a large unaddressed market for AI labs without silicon teams, inference clouds, sovereign AI programs, and enterprises that want to buy dedicated inference chips outright.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, investable market gap — sovereign AI programs, non-hyperscaler labs, and inference clouds — that purchasable custom inference chips could capture.
insights.quote: you can rent a TPU, but you can't buy one, or rack it in your own data center, or build a business on it
insights.locator: Their custom silicon programs were for their workloads

themes.theme: The Etched bet: production as the moat

insights.claim: Etched founders Gavin Uberti, Robert Wachen, and Chris Zhu dropped out of Harvard in 2022 — before ChatGPT existed and years before Cursor, Claude Code, or Codex — to build a full inference system from scratch, including new chips, boards, and interconnects.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Illustrates a founding thesis that predated the current AI boom, which the authors treat as evidence of genuine conviction rather than trend-chasing.
insights.locator: In 2022, months before ChatGPT

insights.claim: Etched has hired more than 400 engineers from Nvidia, Google's TPU group, Broadcom, Apple, SK Hynix, and TSMC, with a striking share working on production — supply chains, rack assembly, burn-in, and logistics — rather than chip design.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Hiring composition signals that in a supply-constrained inference chip market, execution and manufacturing scale-up capability matters as much as chip design talent.
insights.locator: Over the last few years, Etched has hired

insights.claim: Etched's founders describe their scarce advantage as the ability to ship complete, working systems by the thousands rather than just designing a fast chip, summarized in their phrase 'production is the product.'
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Reframes the competitive battleground for inference chip startups from chip architecture to manufacturing and delivery scale, a key differentiator for evaluating rival startups.
insights.locator: As Gavin, Robert, and Chris like to put it

insights.claim: Etched's chip uses 'low-voltage inference,' running math blocks at roughly half the voltage of a typical AI chip, which packs several times more usable compute into the same power envelope.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: A concrete technical mechanism (half-voltage operation) claimed to multiply tokens-per-watt, the key metric the article says determines inference economics.
insights.locator: The first is low-voltage inference

insights.claim: Etched's second core technology is 'cluster-scale memory,' an ultra-low-latency interconnect that pools memory across chips so that during decode an entire rack behaves like one enormous machine.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Addresses the memory-bound bottleneck described earlier in the piece by treating a whole rack, not a single chip, as the unit of inference performance.
insights.locator: The second is cluster-scale memory

insights.claim: Etched's first production chip taped out on TSMC's N4P process and worked on the first attempt ('first-pass silicon'), a rare outcome even for established industry players, achieved by bringing up the chip in under two months versus the industry norm of six to nine months.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: First-pass silicon success and a 3-4x faster bring-up timeline are concrete execution metrics that de-risk Etched's ability to ship on schedule, a key underwriting factor for the investment.
insights.quote: first production chip taped out on TSMC's N4P process and worked on the first attempt
insights.locator: Etched's first production chip taped out

insights.claim: Etched's first hardware racks are shipping to customers in summer 2026, a 10 megawatt site is being stood up, and customers are already running workloads remotely on Etched hardware.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Gives investors a near-term timeline and capacity figure (10MW) to track as an early proof point of Etched's commercialization progress.
insights.locator: The result: those first racks ship to customers this summer

insights.claim: Despite originating from a transformer-focused bet, Etched has built a full-stack inference system capable of serving diverse demanding workloads including many-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts models, state-space models, and long-context agents.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: Broadens Etched's addressable market beyond transformer-only inference, reducing architectural obsolescence risk if the field moves toward MoE or state-space models.
insights.locator: Despite the origin story, what Etched has built

insights.claim: The authors' thesis for backing Etched is that in a market where very few companies can achieve production at scale, the ability to manufacture and ship — not just design — becomes the defensible competitive moat.
insights.speaker: Raghu Raghuram, Sarah Wang
insights.so_what: States a16z's explicit investment rationale: bet on execution/manufacturing capability as the durable moat in inference hardware, not on chip architecture alone.
insights.quote: In a world where production is the product and the machine is the moat, we're thrilled to partner with Etched.
insights.locator: History is unsentimental on this point
